client: I’m really struggling right now. My grandfather passed away recently, and I can’t seem to focus on my final exams, which are starting next week. I feel overwhelmed by grief and guilt, like I should be doing more to honor him, but I also know I need to study. I’m not sure if therapy can even help with something like this—it feels like I just need to push through, but I’m so stuck.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying so much right now—grieving your grandfather while also trying to prepare for exams. I notice you mention feeling stuck between honoring him and studying—can you tell me more about what "honoring him" looks like to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I keep thinking I should be visiting his grave every day or looking through old photos, but then I feel guilty when I don't have time because of studying. He always valued education so much, so part of me thinks studying IS honoring him, but another part feels like that's just an excuse to avoid facing my grief. It's all so confusing.
therapist: You're describing such a painful tug-of-war between what you feel you should do and what you think he would want for you. I notice you're speaking quite quickly—might there be a fear that if you slow down, the grief might feel even bigger?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Yeah...that actually hits home. When I do stop to think about him, it feels like this huge wave of sadness comes over me. So I keep myself distracted with either studying or beating myself up about not grieving "correctly." It's exhausting, but I'm scared if I really let myself feel it, I'll collapse and fail my exams completely.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between two fears - the fear of being overwhelmed by grief if you stop, and the fear of failing if you don't keep going. What would it feel like to experiment with small moments of grieving between study sessions, rather than all-or-nothing approaches?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, moderate-paced speech

client: That actually sounds...less terrifying than what I've been doing. But I worry if I start crying, I won't be able to stop and I'll lose whole study days. Maybe if I set a timer? Though that feels so clinical, like I'm putting grief in a box which seems disrespectful somehow.
therapist: You're describing two very understandable concerns—fear of being consumed by grief, and fear of treating it too clinically. I wonder if we could think of the timer not as a box, but as a way to create space where grief can exist safely alongside your other responsibilities?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That perspective helps a little, but I still feel like I'm doing it wrong somehow. What if I can't even cry when the timer's going? Or what if I do cry and then feel too drained to study right after? I know you're suggesting a middle ground, but it still feels like I'm failing at both grieving and studying.
therapist: It sounds like you're anticipating all the ways this middle path could go wrong—that's the perfectionism we often see in grief. What if, instead of judging each attempt, we simply observed what actually happens in those moments?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I never thought about it as perfectionism before, but that makes sense. It's just...even observation feels scary because what if I observe that I'm terrible at both grieving and studying? Maybe I'm not ready to look that closely yet. But I do see how judging myself before even trying isn't helping.
therapist: You're showing such important self-awareness here—recognizing that even observation feels daunting because it might confirm your fears. Your voice sounds more anxious than your words suggest; is there a part of you that worries if you stop judging yourself harshly, you'll lose your motivation altogether?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, that's exactly it. The self-judgment feels like the only thing keeping me going right now. If I'm not constantly pushing myself, I'm scared I'll just fall apart completely. But at the same time, I'm starting to see how exhausting this constant pressure is—like I'm grieving, studying, and beating myself up all at once.
therapist: Your voice sounds so heavy with exhaustion as you describe this—like the self-judgment that was meant to keep you going is now weighing you down. I wonder if we could explore what "falling apart completely" might actually look like, because right now it seems like the fear of that is keeping you trapped in this exhausting cycle?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: When you ask what "falling apart" looks like...I guess I imagine just lying in bed crying for days, failing all my exams, disappointing everyone who's counting on me. But when I actually think about it, I've had moments of crying already and I didn't completely collapse—I still managed to study after. Maybe the fear is worse than what would actually happen?
therapist: What an important realization—that your actual experience shows you're more resilient than your fears suggest. Your voice sounds softer now as you notice this—what's it like to sit with this realization that your worst fears haven't actually come true in those moments when you've allowed yourself to grieve?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: It's...strangely relieving, but also scary to acknowledge. Part of me wants to hold onto the fear because it feels protective, like if I stop expecting the worst, then the worst might actually happen. But another part of me is tired of carrying this constant dread. I don't know how to trust that I won't fall apart without the fear keeping me in check.
therapist: I hear both hope and hesitation in your voice as you talk about this—the relief of considering you might be more resilient than you thought, mixed with the familiar safety of the fear. That protective part holding onto dread has been working hard for you; what might it need to feel safe enough to loosen its grip a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I think that protective part needs to know I won't completely abandon my responsibilities if I let go a little. But I'm not sure how to prove that to myself—like, what if I try being kinder to myself and then actually do slack off? It feels risky to experiment with this right before exams.
therapist: You're speaking very quickly and softly as you describe this dilemma—it seems there's real tension between wanting to try self-compassion and fearing it might lead to letting everything go. Could we explore what "slacking off" would realistically look like, versus what your anxious part fears it might look like?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech
